HIGHLIGHTS from Chapter 1: 
THE GLOBAL OUTLOOK 
Key Points 
• Global growth is expected to slow  to 2.5 percent in 2026, weaker than previous forecasts , 
before firming to 2.8 percent in 2027–28. 
• Amid surging energy prices, disruptions to commodity markets, and elevated uncertainty, 
growth in emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) is projected to slow 
markedly, especially in commodity importers and those directly affected by the conflict. 
• Successive shocks since 2019, including the ongoing energy crisis, have weighed on per 
capita income growth. EMDEs excluding China and India are on course to experience 
nearly a decade of lost convergence toward advanced‑economy income levels. 
• Risks to the outlook are tilted to the downside. In particular, prolonged disruptions in the 
Strait of Hormuz leading to further increases in energy prices and inflationary pressure, and 
accompanied by financial stress, could leave global growth at just 1.3 percent in 2026. 
• Enhanced global cooperation is needed to safeguard energy and food security, bolster the 
trading system, and advance the energy transition.  
• In many EMDEs, policy makers will need to balance controlling inflation with supporting 
activity, and make efforts to strengthen fiscal sustainability. 
• Bolstering growth and job creation for rising working-age populations requires a concerted 
agenda centered on investing in physical, human, and digital capital; fostering a business -
friendly environment; and mobilizing private investment.  
Global activity:  weaker growth amid soaring energy prices . The global outlook has 
deteriorated, reflecting  surging energy prices, disruptions to commodity markets, elevated 
uncertainty, and tighter monetary conditions. Global growth is expected to decline to 2.5 percent 
this year, with nearly two-thirds of economies facing weaker prospects (figure A). Over 2027–28, 
global growth is expected  to firm to  2.8 percent as energy prices decline, commodity markets 
normalize, financial conditions ease, and trade picks up. The downgrade this year is driven largely 
by emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs), especially commodity importers and 
those directly affected by the conflict (figure B). Nevertheless, several pockets of resilience remain, 
including robust  growth in the United States , strong AI‑related investment , and positive trade 
developments, such as new trade agreements and other unilateral initiatives.  
EMDE outlook: broad-based slowdown. Growth in EMDEs is projected to slow to 3.6 percent 
in 2026—0.4 percentage point below January projections—before firming to 4.2 percent in 2027–
28. The slowdown is expected to vary with exposure to the conflict and related disruptions. China 
is anticipated to decelerate, reflecting declining potential growth, although it remains relatively 
insulated in the near term, supported by strategic reserves, a large share of renewables, and subdued 
inflation. Excluding China, EMDE growth is forec ast to slow from 3.9 percent in 2025 to 3.2 
percent in 2026, before accelerating  to about 4.1 percent in 2027–28 as energy prices ease, 
financial conditions improve, and trade recovers.  Progress in narrowing per capita income gaps 
with advanced economies has stalled across many EMDEs, especially outside China and India, 
pointing to nearly a lost decade of convergence (figure C ). EMDEs face a substantial jobs 
challenge, with about 1.2 billion young people expected to reach working age by 2035.  

 
 
Global Economic Prospects  Global Economic Prospects  Global Economic Prospects  
Risks to the outlook: tilted firmly to the downside.  The outlook is subject to substantial 
downside risks. Growth could be weaker if energy prices surge again amid prolonged disruptions 
in the Strait of Hormuz and inflation accelerates further, with the impact amplified by financial 
stress. Other downside risks include renewed hostilities in the Middle East  or geopolitical flare-
ups elsewhere; escalating trade tensions and policy uncertainty; tighter global financial conditions 
amid rising inflation or fiscal concerns; equity market corrections, particularly in the technology 
sector; and more frequent weather‑related disasters.  On the upside, increased spending on AI -
related investment that broadens across geographies could boost global growth in the short run. In 
the longer term, higher productivity related to effective AI adoption could raise global growth 
(figure D). 
Growth in alternative scenarios: resumption of energy supplies is key. In the baseline, the 
most acute supply disruptions related to the conflict end relatively soon. If the Strait of Hormuz is 
effectively closed to shipping for longer, or if energy production capacity in the Middle East is 
further degraded, energy prices may far exceed baseline projections. In a scenario where prolonged 
disruption leads to the Brent oil price averaging $115/bbl in 2026, global growth could 
underperform by 0.4 percentage point  (figure E). The impacts could be further exacerbated if a 
rise in oil  prices stokes financial market volatility. In this case,  global growth could undershoot 
the baseline by 1.2 percentage point. 
Global policy challenges: mitigate food insecurity, diversify trade , and support energy 
transition. The conflict in the Middle East is set to exacerbate food insecurity, warranting 
coordinated global action to bolster emergency food aid mechanisms (figure F ). Global 
cooperation is also needed to bolster multilateral trading arrangements, deepen and diversify trade 
partnerships, and modernize cross -border investment frameworks, alongside efforts to enhance 
supply chain finance to ease liquidity constraints and reduce non- tariff barriers within regional 
value chains. Accelerating the energy transition is ke y to addressing environmental and energy 
security challenges.  
Near-term domestic policy challenges: calibrate monetary policy and protect  fiscal space. 
EMDE central banks will need to calibrate policy to promote price stability while limiting the drag 
on growth, alongside heightening vigilance to financial stability risks due to shifts in risk appetite. 
Fiscal policy makers need to protect already limited fiscal space amid mounting challenges such 
as elevated debt and borrowing costs, spending on security needs and higher energy prices. Weak 
revenue mobilization, particularly in LICs, is adding to debt sustainability concerns. 
Structural policy challenges: job creation amid AI impacts, and energy security. EMDEs face 
a major jobs challenge as 1.2 billion young people are expected to reach working age by 2035.  
This challenge comes as the effects of AI technologies on labor markets are still unfolding  and 
likely to be uneven across EMDEs. Policy makers can tackle the jobs challenge through a steadfast 
commitment to the fundamentals of long-term growth and job creation. These include greater food 
and energy security, better foundational infrastructure, practical diffusion of technology, and 
openness to trade and diversification, all underpinned by fiscal discipline, strong institutions, 
enabling regulation, investment in human capital , and the catalytic role of private capital 
mobilization.
